claims.text: Controlled annealing at 600–700 °C, combined with in-situ diffraction monitoring, can optimize SRO formation in CoCrNi-based HEAs.
Optimized annealing will produce a uniform SRO state in CoCrNi-based HEAs.
A uniform SRO state will enhance yield strength.
A uniform SRO state will enhance fracture toughness.
A uniform SRO state will enhance ductility.
SRO optimization will maintain a balanced Young’s modulus.
The initial as-cast CoCrNi-based alloy is single-phase and homogeneous.
The initial as-cast alloy contains minimal pre-existing SRO.
In-situ high-energy X-ray diffraction can monitor and validate SRO formation in real time.
Appropriately controlled hold times at 600–700 °C can promote SRO without inducing unwanted phase separation.
Atom probe tomography can confirm and quantify the proposed SRO after annealing.
Uniformly distributed SRO clusters act as localized obstacles to dislocation motion.
Uniformly distributed SRO clusters impede crack propagation.
SRO-induced obstruction of dislocation mobility increases yield strength.
SRO clusters provide crack deflection that improves fracture resistance.
Optimized SRO can preserve or slightly improve ductility while increasing strength and fracture resistance.
The treatment will improve yield strength by at least 10–15% relative to state-of-the-art CoCrNi-based HEAs.
The treatment will improve fracture toughness by at least 10–15% relative to state-of-the-art CoCrNi-based HEAs.
State-of-the-art CoCrNi-based HEAs use standard heat treatments that lack precise SRO control.
Phase separation, microstructural heterogeneity, or deviations in annealing temperature or time will diminish the proposed benefits.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says ductility will be enhanced, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome permit ductility merely to be preserved or maintained.
